# MyPyStub

**This cross-platform app was generated by [Briefcase](https://briefcase.readthedocs.io/) - part of [The BeeWare Project](https://beeware.org/). If you want to see more tools like Briefcase, please consider [becoming a financial member of BeeWare](https://beeware.org/contributing/membership).**

My first application for prototyping with iDevices and Python

This application is mainly tested on iPhone and iPad, and uses the iOS limited subset of *Toga*. Android is experimental: it builds and runs on Android devices and emulators, but is tested less. It is intended to act as a stub to enable you to install an up-to-date Python interpreter to your device for free. (Apple allows any account to become a Developer account for free that can install up to three apps that are re-deployed once every seven days.)

If you compile and deploy this app on iOS, it will create a "MyPyStub" folder in your Files app under "On My iPhone" (or "On My iPad"). On Android, the app's folder appears in your device's file browser.

You may place Python scripts in there. Either place bare scripts, or place modules in folders. Modules should have a `pyproject.toml` file to nominate any pure-Python dependencies that will attempt to be downloaded from PyPI at runtime.

Only a minimum of packages are preinstalled (if you build this yourself you can pre-install packages by adjusting the *Briefcase* configuration).

## Writing prototypes

The launcher lists your scripts and project folders; tap one to run it. *This lets one of your three free app slots hold many Python prototypes.* Scripts run as they would with `python script.py`, so the same file also works on a desktop, or as a standalone app built with *Briefcase*. Put their start-up code under `if __name__ == "__main__":`.

| Mode | When the run ends | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Plain script (`print`, `input`) | when the script returns | `basics/hello_world.py`, `basics/hello_you.py` |
| Long-running script | when its work finishes | `threads/countdown.py` |
| Main-thread work | when the script returns | `threads/main_thread.py` |
| Arguments and environment variables (set by swiping right for **Setup**) | when the script returns | `basics/args_and_env.py`, `basics/show_args.py`, `basics/show_env.py` |
| Dependencies (PEP 723) | installed first, then as above | `basics/with_dependency.py` |
| Project folder (`pyproject.toml`) | as for its entry point | `basics/hello_project/` |
| Entry points (`[project.scripts]`, `gui-scripts`, other groups) | as for a script; several open like a folder | `projects/two_tools/` |
| Taking over the screen with Toga | when it hands the screen back | `takeover/back_button.py`, `takeover/nested_takeover.py` |

Swipe left on a row for **Info** (a folder's README; a script's docstring, dependencies and source; a project's metadata, README, licence and changelog), and right for **Setup**, which sets its arguments and environment variables, saving as you go. Variables set on the Setup tab's **Environment** page are inherited by every run. The in-app Help page explains each one (see "How your script is run"), and the examples are in the app's **Examples** category. Your own modules are reloaded on each run, so edits take effect without restarting the app.

This is purely experimental at this stage but you're welcome to experiment with it!

## Development

Desktop development uses [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/):

```bash
uv sync
```

```bash
uv run pre-commit install
```

The pre-commit hooks run the same checks as the pull request gate (`.github/workflows/pr-gate.yml`): `ruff check`, `pyright`, and `pytest`. To run them by hand:

```bash
uv run pre-commit run --all-files
```

## Building an Android APK by hand, with another Python

Fastlane (below) builds the release APK with the default Python. To build one by hand, for example with Python 3.14 beside the default build, run Briefcase under the Python you want: it picks the Android Python from the interpreter that runs it. Give each Python its own app ID so the APKs install side by side without clashing. `app_name` can't be overridden (and it names the module Briefcase starts), so change the **bundle**, which comes before it in the app ID, and the **formal name**, which is the name under the icon. Briefcase reads each `-C` value as TOML, so a string needs quotes inside the quotes. The documents provider's authority follows the app ID, so two installs can both appear in the Files app.

`scripts/build_android.py` does all of this: it generates the icons (only the original is in Git, and without creating all of the variants the app gets Briefcase's default), writes the build info (so About shows your branch), clears the old build, runs `create` and `package -p apk` under that Python with the right `-C` options, and signs the APK if you have set the signing variables (below). Without a version it builds the default Python (currently 3.15, but whatever your Briefcase is running), named the same way. Add `--plain` to keep the normal app ID and name (`au.id.jking.mypystub`, "MyPyStub"), which updates a Fastlane build instead of installing beside it. _Note that this process assumes that you use `uv`!_

```bash
uv run scripts/build_android.py 3.14
```

That app's ID is `au.id.jking.py314.mypystub`. The result is in `dist/`. Briefcase leaves the APK with an awkward (generic or with spaces) name, so the script renames it to `MyPyStub_314-<version>.apk` (the Python without its dot, then the version) and signs it into `MyPyStub_314-<version>-signed.apk`. Without signing variables only the **unsigned** one is made, and Android refuses to install it until it is signed. `apksigner` also writes a `.idsig` file beside the signed APK, which installing doesn't need. The script uses `-p apk` because Briefcase's default is an `.aab` for Google Play.

By hand, the steps are: `uv run generate_icons.py`; `uv run scripts/build_info.py`; `rm -rf build/mypystub/android` (Briefcase won't overwrite it, and every Python builds into that folder); then `briefcase create android` and `briefcase package android -p apk` under `uvx --python 3.14`, each with `-C 'bundle="au.id.jking.py314"' -C 'formal_name="MyPyStub 3.14"'`, and the same options on any other Briefcase command you run.

For a quick test on your own device, `briefcase build android` (with the same `-C` options) makes a debug-signed APK that `adb install -r` accepts. Don't hand that one to anyone else: it is debuggable, and a debug key from another machine can't update it.

### Signing the APK by hand

Briefcase 0.4 doesn't sign Android packages. You need a keystore, made once, and the Android SDK's `apksigner`. **Keep the keystore and its passwords safe, and out of the repository.** Every later build must be signed with the same key, or phones will refuse to update an installed copy. It is the same key Fastlane uses (`ANDROID_KEYSTORE` and the other `ANDROID_KEY*` variables), so a hand-signed APK can update a Fastlane build of the same app ID.

**If you are going to do this, you probably should change `bundle` in `pyproject.toml` to one of your own (effectively indicating a _fork_).**

Make a keystore, only if you don't have one:

```bash
keytool -genkeypair -v -keystore ~/mypystub.jks -alias mypystub -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000
```

`scripts/build_android.py` signs for you when these are set (it reads the passwords from the environment, so `apksigner` doesn't stop to ask): `ANDROID_KEYSTORE`, `ANDROID_KEY_ALIAS`, `ANDROID_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD`, and `ANDROID_KEY_PASSWORD` only if the key has its own password. To sign by hand instead, sign the APK (use the newest folder under `build-tools`; `$ANDROID_HOME` is usually `~/Library/Android/sdk` on a Mac). It asks for the passwords:

```bash
"$ANDROID_HOME"/build-tools/<version>/apksigner sign --ks ~/mypystub.jks --ks-key-alias mypystub --out dist/MyPyStub-signed.apk dist/<the unsigned>.apk
```

Check the signature, then install it on a connected phone or emulator, or send the signed file to testers:

```bash
"$ANDROID_HOME"/build-tools/<version>/apksigner verify --verbose dist/MyPyStub-signed.apk
```

```bash
"$ANDROID_HOME"/platform-tools/adb install -r dist/MyPyStub-signed.apk
```

Installing over an app that was signed with a different key fails with a signature mismatch; uninstall it first (this deletes its data).

## Releasing to TestFlight

Builds are shipped by hand from a clone on a Mac with Xcode, Ruby, and Bundler. The `Continuous Delivery to TestFlight` workflow only runs `fastlane ios share` and is manual; on a Mac it costs no CI minutes.

```bash
bundle install
```

Export the App Store Connect API key and team details (keep these out of the repository):

- `APP_STORE_CONNECT_KEY_ID`
- `APP_STORE_CONNECT_ISSUER_ID`
- `APP_STORE_CONNECT_PRIVATE_KEY`
- `APP_STORE_TEAM_ID`

Then run one of the lanes in `fastlane/Fastfile`:

```bash
bundle exec fastlane ios share
```

- `share` builds and uploads to TestFlight. TestFlight's "What to Test" is the newest build's section of What's New, not the git log. The build goes to your **internal** testers, which Apple doesn't review, like the `internal` group on Firebase App Distribution for Android.
- `bundle exec fastlane ios share external:"Beta Testers"` (or `TESTFLIGHT_EXTERNAL_GROUPS="Beta Testers,Friends"` in the environment) also submits the build to those **external** TestFlight groups. Apple reviews external builds (Beta App Review): the first build of a new version is reviewed, which with a calver version is the first build of each day, and a build can wait in review before testers get it. So it is opt-in per release, not the default. It needs the groups to exist in App Store Connect, and the app's Test Information (contact details and notes) filled in there. Works with `upload` and `both` too.
- `bundle exec fastlane both` (from `main`) ships iOS and Android together. It checks the iOS and Android environment first, then builds **both** apps, and only then uploads to TestFlight and Firebase App Distribution, so if either build fails neither platform gets one. The uploads themselves still run one after the other: if TestFlight succeeds and Firebase then fails, the lane tags the build number as used and stops, and the Android build has to be uploaded again (`fastlane android upload` makes a new build with the next number).
- `bundle exec fastlane android local` builds the APK signed with your release key and installs it on a connected device or emulator, then starts it, in place of `briefcase run android`. Because it is signed like the Firebase build and numbered like a release, it installs over a Firebase build, keeping its data. It needs only the `ANDROID_KEY*` signing variables, uploads nothing and pushes no tag. With several devices attached, name one: `bundle exec fastlane android local device:<serial>` (or set `ANDROID_SERIAL`); `adb devices -l` lists the serials. Its log is in `adb logcat`, or the app's Logs tab.
- `mirror` copies `main` and its release tags to the public repository (`bundle exec fastlane mirror`; set `PUBLIC_REPO_URL` to override the remote). `share` runs it after tagging, so the About page's Source link works in the public repository; run it by hand to catch up after merging.
- `local` builds and installs on local devices.
- `manual` builds the Xcode project and leaves signing and deploying to Xcode.

The `share` lane also collects the change fragments in `changes/` into the app's Help → What's New page and commits them (see `changes/README.md`).

Fastlane sets the version, so do not edit it by hand. Before Briefcase runs, it picks today's date and the next build number, one more than the highest already used today, and `scripts/set_version.py` stamps them into `pyproject.toml` (restored afterwards). Python sees the build number as a fourth number, so the version is plain PEP 440 with no words. Xcode's version keys hold at most three numbers, so it keeps the build number apart. Every lane numbers its build the same way:

| | Example |
|---|---|
| Python (`app.version`, About page) | `2026.11.2.3` |
| Xcode `CFBundleShortVersionString` | `2026.11.2` |
| Xcode `CFBundleVersion` | `3` |

The build number comes from **GitHub, not App Store Connect**: one more than the highest `YYYY.M.D.N` tag on `origin` for today (Fastlane fetches the tags first), and any such release on the public repository's GitHub Releases (read anonymously, best effort). Every lane that uploads a build also tags it, `upload` lanes included, so a number is never used twice. A build uploaded some other way (from Xcode, say) isn't tagged, so tag it by hand (`git tag 2026.11.2.4 && git push origin 2026.11.2.4`) or its number could be used again, and TestFlight and Android both reject that.

Runs straight from the source tree (`briefcase dev`, tests) show the placeholder version in `pyproject.toml`.

After a successful upload, `share` tags the commit with the Python version (for example `2026.11.2.3`) and pushes the tag. The `mirror` lane copies `main` and the release tags on `main` to the public repository, and the About page links to the tag of the running build ("Source"). Tags on commits that aren't on `main` stay private, so share from `main`; a build from a branch that is later squash-merged keeps a private tag, and the lane warns about it. 

### Which branch a build came from

Fastlane runs `scripts/build_info.py` before every build. It writes the branch and `git describe` to `src/mypystub/resources/build_info.json` (ignored by Git), which Briefcase bundles, and the About page shows them for builds that aren't from `main`. Before a local `briefcase run`, run it yourself, or About shows whatever an older build left there:

```bash
uv run scripts/build_info.py
```

A run from the source tree on a desktop (`briefcase dev`) asks Git directly.

### GitHub Releases

After the tag is mirrored, `share` creates a **GitHub Release** for it on the public repository (`PUBLIC_REPOSITORY`, default `jkingok/mypystub`). Its title is the version and its body is that build's *What's New* text, the same Markdown the app shows (`scripts/collect_changes.py --release-notes <version>`). The About page's *Source* link opens that Release page, which also leads to the code at the tag.

Creating a Release needs `GITHUB_RELEASE_TOKEN`, a token allowed to write Releases on the public repository. Keep it in the environment with the App Store Connect keys, never in the repository. (Fastlane's `set_github_release` takes it as its `api_token` argument; its own environment variable would be `FL_GITHUB_RELEASE_API_TOKEN`, but this repository reads `GITHUB_RELEASE_TOKEN` and passes it in.) Without it `share` warns and skips the Release, since the upload has already happened; make it later with:

```bash
bundle exec fastlane release version:2026.11.8.1
```

#### Making a token (desktop or CI)

Use a fine-grained personal access token limited to the public repository:

1. GitHub → Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → **Fine-grained tokens** → Generate new token.
2. Resource owner `jkingok`; **Only select repositories**: `jkingok/mypystub`.
3. Repository permissions: **Contents: Read and write** (what creating a Release needs; Metadata read-only is added for you).
4. Pick an expiry, generate, and copy the token (it is shown once).
5. On the Mac, `export GITHUB_RELEASE_TOKEN=...` in the shell profile or keychain-backed secrets, then run the `release` lane above. In CI, store it as a repository secret.

A classic token with the `public_repo` scope also works but reaches all your public repositories. Check GitHub's [managing personal access tokens](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/managing-your-personal-access-tokens) page for the current steps; these were written from memory.
